title: TCP Extensions for High Performance
summary: Presents TCP extensions to improve performance over paths with large bandwidth-delay products and to give reliable operation over very high-speed paths. It defines new TCP options for this purpose. It was replaced by RFC 7323.

plainLanguage.summary: Plain TCP is like a pipe where you wait for each reply. These options let TCP keep much more data in flight on long fast links, so the pipe stays full.

questions: what is the tcp timestamps option
subtitle: Window scaling, timestamps and PAWS: modest TCP options that keep fast, long paths full and reliable.

tldr.problem: TCP's 16-bit window field caps the data in flight at about 65K bytes, round-trip timing samples only one packet per window, and a 32-bit sequence space can wrap around within the time an old segment lingers on a very fast path.
tldr.mechanism: Three new TCP options fix this: Window Scale multiplies the advertised window by a power of two, Timestamps lets almost every segment give an RTT measurement (RTTM), and the same timestamps let a receiver reject old duplicates (PAWS).
tldr.outcome: This memo combined and replaced RFC 1072 and RFC 1185. It has since been obsoleted by RFC 7323.

facts.label: Timestamp size
facts.value: 32 bits each for TSval and TSecr

facts.label: Idle invalidation
facts.value: TS.Recent invalidated after more than 24 days idle

sections.title: Long Fat Pipes and Fast Wraparound
sections.content:
TCP performance depends on the bandwidth*delay product, the amount of unacknowledged data needed to keep a path full. The RFC calls a path where this is large a "long, fat pipe" or LFN (pronounced "elephan(t)"). For example, a cross-country delay of 30 ms at DS3 bandwidth (45Mbps) already exceeds 106 bits.

The memo names three performance problems on an LFN:

  • Window size limit: the 16-bit window field limits the window to 216 = 65K bytes.
  • Recovery from losses: more than one loss per window typically forces a timeout and slow start. Selective acknowledgments would help, but SACK was omitted from this memo because its format and semantics still needed work.
  • Round-trip measurement: sampling one packet per window gives a poor RTT estimate on an LFN and can cause spurious retransmissions.

There is also a reliability problem. TCP depends on a bound on segment lifetime (MSL), but a 32-bit sequence number can wrap within that time at high enough speed. The memo requires 231 / B to exceed the MSL, where B is bandwidth in bytes per second. The culprit is high bandwidth rather than large windows.
sections.plainLanguage: If a long garden hose can only hold one cup at a time, it stays mostly empty. Fast, long network links are like that hose, and the numbering on the water cups can also run out and start repeating.

sections.title: The Window Scale Option
sections.content:
The Window Scale option expands the window to 32 bits by carrying a scale factor next to the 16-bit Window field. It is three bytes long: Kind=3, Length=3 and a one-byte shift.cnt. It may be sent only in a SYN segment, so the scale is fixed in each direction when the connection opens.

The option is an offer, not a promise: both sides must send it in their SYN segments to enable scaling in either direction. A shift.cnt of zero means offering to scale with a factor of 1. The Window field in a SYN segment itself is never scaled.

A receiving TCP left-shifts the Window field of each incoming non-SYN segment by the sender's shift count to get the true window. The shift count is limited to 14, which allows windows of 230 bytes (1 Gbyte); if a larger value arrives, the TCP should log the error and use 14. Windows are kept locally as 32-bit values, and the congestion window is not affected by the scale factor.
sections.plainLanguage: The scoreboard only has room for small numbers, so both teams agree at the start that every number shown means, say, 16 times that. Then the scoreboard can show much bigger scores.

sections.title: Timestamps and Round-Trip Time Measurement
sections.content:
The Timestamps option is Kind=8, Length=10 bytes, with two four-byte fields: TSval (the sender's timestamp clock) and TSecr (the echo of a timestamp received from the peer; valid only when the ACK bit is set, otherwise zero). A TCP may send it in an initial SYN and may use it on other segments only if the peer sent it in its SYN.

With RTTM the sender stamps its segments and the receiver reflects the stamp in ACKs, so a single subtraction gives an RTT measurement for nearly every ACK, including after retransmissions. A TSecr is used to update the averaged RTT only if the segment acknowledges new data, so idle gaps do not inflate the estimate.

When several timestamps arrive before a reply, the receiver keeps one, TS.Recent. If Last.ACK.sent falls within the range of an incoming segment's sequence numbers, that segment's TSval is copied to TS.Recent. This echoes the earliest unacknowledged segment under delayed ACKs, the last in-order segment when there is a hole, and the segment that fills a hole.
sections.plainLanguage: Put the time on each letter. The friend writes your stamp back on the reply, and you can see how long the round trip took without guessing.

sections.title: PAWS: Rejecting Old Duplicates
sections.content:
PAWS (Protect Against Wrapped Sequence numbers) uses the same timestamps. Timestamps are 32-bit unsigned values in a modular space, and a segment can be discarded as an old duplicate if its TSval is less than the timestamp recently received on the connection. In the basic algorithm, if a segment has a Timestamps option, SEG.TSval < TS.Recent, and TS.Recent is valid, the receiver sends an ACK and drops the segment. The check is made when a segment first arrives, not again when queued segments are delivered.

No clock synchronization is needed; the receiver treats the timestamp as a logical extension of the high-order bits of the sequence number. The timestamp clock must tick at least once per 231 bytes sent, and its recycle time must exceed the MSL. The memo chooses a clock frequency in the range 1 ms to 1 sec per tick.

If a connection is idle for more than 24 days, the saved TS.Recent could become too old, so an implementation MUST invalidate it in that case. RST segments should not carry timestamps and are acceptable regardless of timestamp. With header prediction, the timestamp check is recommended to come first.
sections.plainLanguage: Each letter gets a number that only goes up. If a letter shows up with an older number than one you already have, it is a leftover copy and you throw it away.

sections.title: Compatibility, Overhead and Security
sections.content:
All three extensions are new TCP options. The only previously defined option, MSS, appears only on SYN segments, and some buggy TCPs might crash on an option in a non-SYN segment. So these options are sent on non-SYN segments only after both sides have exchanged them in the SYN segments, and a SYN,ACK carries an extension option only if the SYN did.

A Timestamps option adds 12 bytes to the 20-byte TCP header on any data or ACK segment. The memo expects the bandwidth saved by fewer unnecessary retransmissions to repay this, and Appendix A recommends an aligned option layout for fast parsing. For low-speed networks, the extensions might be left off.

The memo also discusses duplicates from earlier incarnations of a connection, which are handled by the usual MSL rules rather than PAWS. Its Security Considerations section says only that security issues are not discussed.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides have to say "I know the new trick" before anyone uses it, so old computers are not confused. The extra labels do make each letter slightly heavier.
